title: Time-optimal robust quantum control for partially known errors
abstract: Robust quantum control usually assumes one of two extremes: the error is of a known form and only its strength is unknown, or nothing at all is known about it. In practice one often sits in between. The size of a static error is unknown, but its class is known, for example, it only shifts energy levels, or it acts on each subsystem separately. We ask how fast a control can cancel, to first order, every error in such a class. A time-independent Hamiltonian can do this if and only if all errors in the class have zero diagonal in a common basis. In that case an equally spaced energy ladder in this basis does it after one period. A lower bound that holds for any time-dependent control with bounded drive power shows that this simple constant control is optimal for several natural classes, including unknown level shifts and unknown local errors on two subsystems. Completely unknown errors need a time-dependent control, and there, knowing the error class shortens the minimum time by a factor $\sqrt{d^2+1}$. So partial knowledge of the error changes not only how long an optimal robust control takes, but also its form.
summary: This theoretical paper investigates time-optimal robust quantum control when the noise error is only partially known. It shows that knowing the structure of the error class allows for the use of simple, constant control Hamiltonians that achieve the minimum possible control time. This finding is vital for designing practical quantum gates in noisy environments.
main_problem: The paper determines the minimum time required for a bounded quantum control drive to robustly cancel, to first order, errors belonging to a partially known class $S$.
main_result: Partial knowledge of the error class allows for a time-independent (constant) Hamiltonian to achieve the global minimum time, significantly reducing the required control duration compared to completely unknown errors.
method: The analysis uses first-order error expansion (Magnus expansion) and derives lower bounds for the control time by analyzing the signal overlap matrix (Gram matrix) of the system's time evolution signals.
model_or_system: The system is a $d$-level quantum system subjected to a control Hamiltonian $H(t)$ and a small static error $\epsilon X$, where $X$ belongs to a known class $S$. The control aims to make the first-order error integral vanish.
key_observables: Minimum time ($\Omega T$), Infidelity ($1-F$), and the scaling exponent ($p$) of the infidelity with the error strength $\epsilon$.
important_parameters: The dimension $d$ of the system, the error strength $\epsilon$, and the control power bound $\Omega$.
main_assumptions: The analysis is restricted to first-order error cancellation, and the control drive is assumed to be bounded and measurable in time.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate constant controls for various partially known error classes (e.g., qubit plane, qutrit level shifts) and compare the minimum duration against the case of completely unknown errors.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the general robustness condition ($\int U^\dagger X U dt = 0$) to deriving lower bounds using signal analysis (Gram matrix) and finally demonstrating that constant controls are optimal for several natural, partially known error classes.
why_interesting: This work provides concrete, quantitative results on how partial knowledge of noise structure can be exploited to design significantly faster and more efficient quantum control protocols, which is crucial for practical quantum computation.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Constant controls for partially known errors. (a) Horizontal lines are the energy levels of the constant control Hamiltonian, spaced by 2π/T. Arrows are the matrix elements of the possible errors in that basis. Since every error has zero diagonal there, each component connects two different levels; in the frame moving with the control it oscillates at a nonzero multiple of 2π/T and integrates to zero over one period (the arrows are oscillating matrix elements, not transitions). Left: a qubit error confined to a plane, cancelled by a 2π rotation about the normal ˆn. Middle: unknown level shifts of a qutrit, cancelled by a Hamiltonian diagonal in the Fourier basis |fk⟩, a chiral drive...

FIG. 2. Robust control as refocusing. (a,b) Ensembles of systems, each with its own random static error from the stated class (root-mean-square strength ϵ = 0.1 Ω). The curves show the ensemble-averaged fidelity | tr(U † 0Uϵ)/d|2 between the actual and ideal evolution; vertical lines mark the control periods. (a) Qutrits with unknown level shifts: without control (dashed) the ensemble dephases, while the constant chiral drive (15) refocuses it at every period T = 4π/Ω.
